### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
Most famous mathematicians first showed a strong interest in mathematics around middle school age. For example, John Todd (1911–2007), a well-known international leader in numerical mathematics, said, “My mathematical career started in the following way. I was in a class, a singing class. My singing was so bad the teacher said I was disturbing the class and had to leave! There were some extra classes, ones with national examinations. And so I had to be put in one of them—it was a second-year algebra class! That’s when I started learning mathematics.”[[14]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn14)
Another mathematician, Jenny Harrison, currently a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, was primarily interested in nature and music during her teen years. In an interview with John-Steiner, she recalled her beginnings. Jenny Harrison was born in Atlanta, Georgia, and spent most of her time outside of school in the woods. This attraction to the natural world may have influenced Harrison throughout her life and can be seen in the way she explores mathematical landscapes. She talked about her visual view of the world and her enjoyment in exploring paths in the woods. This strong preference may well have contributed to her later interests in geometry. The influence and encouragement of her older brother contributed to her strength and self-confidence. He got Harrison interested in basic problems in physics when they were teenagers.[[15]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn15)
texts.19:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
Although she clearly showed an aptitude for math early on (scoring the highest in her state in a take-home competition), her primary passion was for music. She studied the piano and believed for most of her adolescence that she would devote her life to it. Music is still a part of her life, but Harrison is basically a shy person and found that she was uncomfortable performing in public. “I knew I didn’t want to do music and I went over and shut the lid to the piano. I was intrigued by three problems and wanted to try to understand them: the nature of consciousness, time and light. The question was how best to do this. I eventually settled on mathematics as I felt it would give me answers I could trust.”[[16]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn16)
Julia Robinson (1919–1985), who became famous for helping to prove that Hilbert’s 10th problem is unsolvable (specifically, that there is no formula or computer program that can always decide whether an arbitrary polynomial equation with whole number coefficients has a whole-number solution) wrote, “One of my earliest memories is of arranging pebbles in the shadow of a giant saguaro, squinting because the sun was so bright. I think that I have always had a basic liking for natural numbers. To me they are the one real thing.”[[17]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn17)
texts.20:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
Sophie Germain (1776–1831), who was to make an important contribution to proving Fermat’s Last Theorem, was born in Paris. As a girl, she had to fight hard for the right to read mathematics. Her interest in mathematics began at age 13, during the French Revolution. Because of the battles going on in the streets of Paris, Sophie was confined to her home, where she spent a lot of time in her father’s library. There she read about the death of Archimedes. It is said that on the day that his city, Syracuse, was being overrun by the Romans, Archimedes was engrossed in a geometric figure in the sand and ignored the questioning of a Roman soldier. As a result, he was speared to death.[[18]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn18) If someone could be so engrossed in a problem as to ignore a soldier and die for it, thought Sophie, the subject must be interesting.
Sophie began teaching herself mathematics, using the books in her father’s library. Her parents did all they could to discourage her. She began studying at night to escape them, but they went to such measures as taking away her clothes once she was in bed and depriving her of heat and light to make her stay in her bed at night instead of studying. Sophie’s parents’ efforts failed. She would wrap herself in quilts and use candles she had hidden in order to study at night. Finally her parents realized that Sophie’s passion for mathematics was “incurable,” and they let her learn. Thus Sophie spent the years of the Reign of Terror studying differential calculus without the aid of a tutor![[19]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn19)
texts.21:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
Sofia Kovalevskaya (1850–1891) was the first woman to achieve full status as a professional mathematician. Born in Moscow in 1850, her interest in mathematics was stimulated in childhood by the wallpaper in her nursery. Kovalevskaya wrote, “When we moved to the country from Kaluga the whole house was painted and papered. The wallpaper had been ordered from St. Petersburg, but the quantity needed was not estimated quite accurately, so that paper was lacking for one room. Considering that all the other rooms were in order the nursery might well manage without special paper.”[[20]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn20) Some paper that was lying around in the attic was used for the purpose. By a happy chance the paper for this covering consisted of the lithographed calculus lectures of the analyst M. V. Ostrogradsky that her father had acquired as a young man. “It amused me to examine these sheets, yellowed by time, all speckled over with some kind of hieroglyphics whose meaning escaped me completely but which, I felt, must signify something very wise and interesting. And I would stand by the wall for hours, reading and rereading what was written there. I remember particularly that on the sheet of paper which happened to be in the most prominent place on the wall, there was an explanation of the concepts of infinitesimals and limits.”[[21]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn21)
Figure 1-1. Sofia Kovalevskaya, pioneer Russian analyst. © Institut Mittag-Leffle
Kovalevskaya recalled her uncle speaking to her about the quadrature of the circle: “If the meaning of his words was unintelligible to me, they struck my imagination and inspired me with a kind of veneration for mathematics, as for a superior, mysterious science, opening to its initiates a new and marvelous world inaccessible to the ordinary mortal.”[[22]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn22)
texts.22:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
Kovalevskaya, too, had to overcome the resistance of her family. In fact, in order to study mathematics, she had to leave Russia for Germany. To do this legally, she had to marry, and so at age 18 she married “in name only,” another idealistic student, Vladimir Kovalevskii.
The Uruguayan mathematician José Luis Massera (1915–2002), who in his fifties became an international cause célèbre as a political prisoner, described his discovery of mathematics as “a revolution.” Massera wrote:
When I was fifteen the revolution began in my home which lasted for several years. My father had a Hispanic American Encylopedic Dictionary of several volumes and of sufficiently high level. One day, on returning from German class, it occurred to me to look in the dictionary for one of the words that had been used, probably “equation.” I found myself with an enormous quantity of different equations, whose existence I hadn’t even suspected, nor how to approach them. My curiosity being amply satisfied with the algebraic equations, I went to look for one of the others of the dictionary. Thus, day by day and word by word, I began a review, entirely chaotic, no doubt, that was providing me with a harvest of mathematical terms and valuable information about them that I was accumulating and conceptualizing slowly.
During a family trip they passed through Paris where he accompanied his father to a great bookstore. There they found two books: one on classical geometry and the other on trigonometry. Massera devoured them in a short time. He liked the way the material was sequenced and practiced. Subsequently, with the help of a dictionary, he began to read a larger volume on projective geometry. He met his colleague and lifelong friend Rafael Laguardia in high school. He and Laguardia established a study group of young people interested in mathematics and shared their knowledge with them and each other.[[23]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn23)
texts.23:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
One of the most astounding childhood accomplishments in mathematics was achieved by Louis Joel Mordell (1888–1972), who was chair of the math department at the University of Manchester from 1922 to 1945, and then successor to G. H. Hardy in the Sadleirian chair at Cambridge University. This pillar of English pure mathematics was a self-taught boy from Philadelphia. He was the third of eight children of a Hebrew scholar. Louis became fascinated by mathematics while in grade school. He learned on his own, buying second-hand mathematics books from a bookstore in Philadelphia for 5 or 10 cents when he was 13 years old. These books contained problems from the Cambridge tripos examinations (written tests for undergraduates), so Louis came to think of Cambridge University in England as the mathematical summit. He later wrote, “I conceived what can only be described as a thoroughly mad and crazy idea of going to Cambridge and trying for a scholarship. . . . I had no idea of the necessary standards. I was self-taught mathematically and had never participated in a competitive examination.”[[24]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn24) He earned the money for his passage to England by tutoring his fellow pupils for 7 hours a day. In December 1906 he went to Cambridge and competed in the university scholarship exam. He placed first! He could only afford a one-word telegram back to his father. It read simply, “Hurrah.”
texts.24:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
The Russian, Israel Moiseevich Gelfand (1913–2009), is one of the most illustrious mathematicians of the 20th century. In the small town near Odessa where he grew up, there was only one school. The mathematics teacher there was very kind, but Israel Moiseyevich quickly surpassed him. Gelfand said, “My parents could not order books in mathematics for me; they had no money. But I became lucky. When I was 15 my parents brought me to Odessa for an appendectomy. I said that I wouldn’t go to the hospital unless they bought me a book on mathematics.”[[25]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn25) Before he read that book, he had thought that algebra and geometry were two different mathematical subjects. When he saw Maclaurin’s formula for the sine, he suddenly realized that there was no gap between the two. “Mathematics became united. And since then I understood that different areas of mathematics together with mathematical physics formed a single whole.”[[26]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn26)
Figure 1-2. Israel M. Gelfand, one of the foremost mathematicians of his time. © Mariana Cook 1990.
texts.25:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Mathematicians’ Early Teen Years
Andrew Wiles, who is now famous for proving Fermat’s Last Theorem, first became fascinated by that problem at the age of 10. He loved doing math problems in school and would take them home and make up new ones of his own.[[27]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn27) When he was 10, Andrew found Fermat’s Last Theorem in Eric Temple Bell’s classic Men of Mathematics. Thirty years later, Wiles remembered, “It looked so simple, and yet all the great mathematicians in history couldn’t solve it. Here was a problem that I, a ten-year-old, could understand and I knew from that moment that I would never let it go. I had to solve it.”[[28]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn28)
texts.26:
### 1. Mathematical Beginnings
#### Psychological Themes
David Feldman, a developmental psychologist at Tufts University, studied child prodigies and didn’t find many prodigies under the age of 10. He wrote, “Mathematics fosters far fewer prodigies than I thought would be the case when this work began.”[[29]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn29) With the help of Julian Stanley at Johns Hopkins University, he did identify Billy Devlin. When Devlin was 6 he scored in the high school range on the Scholastic Aptitude Test. He became one of the participants in Feldman’s study at age 7. But as he grew older, he turned away from mathematics to physics and astronomy.
Recently, Terence Tao received international attention as a 2006 Fields Medal winner. “Terry is like Mozart; mathematics just flows out of him,” said John Garnett, professor and former chair of mathematics at the University of California, Los Angeles, “except without Mozart’s personality problems; everyone likes him. Mathematicians with Terry’s talent appear only once in a generation. . . . He’s an incredible talent, and probably the best mathematician in the world right now.”[[30]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn30) He is a prodigy who started to play with numbers at 2 years of age. His father, Billy Tao, is a pediatrician who, together with his mother, carefully supported their child’s great gift. They were successful in setting up an individualized program for him where he was able to acquire each subject at his own pace, quickly accelerating through several grades of math and science while remaining closer to his age group in other subjects.[[31]](https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/reuben-hersh-and-vera-john-steiner-loving-hating-mathematics#fn31) His home environment was supportive, and today he continues this legacy by being a thoughtful and devoted parent. At the same time, he produces an extraordinary range of important mathematics. He is a wonderful counterexample to the popular image of the eccentric mathematician.

### DIAMOND JUBILARIANS
The following Diamond Jubilarians are celebrating 70 years in religious life with the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
They entered the BVM Congregation on Sept. 8, 1956. They professed first vows on Feb. 3, 1959, and final vows July 16, 1964.

## MIGUEL (MARY MIGUEL) CONWAY, BVM
Miguel Conway, BVM often says she learned community before she could name it.
“I am the third of eight Conway children,” she says. “Four girls, four boys. We all had the experience of a close-knit community from infancy.”
**Rooted in Family and Faith**
Growing up in Boone, Iowa, during the years surrounding World War II meant learning responsibility early. When her father, William, went to war, Miguel and her siblings grew up fast with the help of a strong mother who emphasized faith and family.
That faith was nurtured in classrooms staffed by the BVMs. Miguel’s mother, Kathryn, herself educated by the BVMs, was convinced that they were “the best educators in the world,” Miguel says.
**Faith, Music, and Laughter**
In Boone, a largely non-Catholic town, the sisters’ presence offered both academic rigor and ecumenical openness with the town’s residents.
“The BVM Sisters were known and loved in the community by everybody,” Miguel remembers.
Two teachers left a lasting mark: Sister Mary Leonilda Kerrigan and Sister Mary Gregory Berchmans.
“They taught us to trust in God, to pray, to think, to calculate, and to challenge the issues of our day,” Miguel says.
Music, laughter, and faith filled the Conway home. Miguel and her sisters Pat and Judy became known as “The Conway Trio,” singing and playing instruments at church. They attended daily Mass, and the family gathered weekly to watch Bishop Fulton Sheen on the household’s first television.
After high school, college was the natural next step. Miguel headed off to Clarke University in Dubuque, Iowa, to study math and education.
**A Call That Couldn’t Wait**
A family tragedy sharpened her sense of urgency to begin her vocation. After her brother Mick was killed in an auto accident, Miguel felt she couldn’t ignore it any longer.
“I began to think that it isn’t a good idea to put important things off,” she says. “I knew, even then, that God was calling me to religious life.”
She entered the BVM Community supported wholeheartedly by her parents.
**A Family of Families in Ecuador**

## MIGUEL (MARY MIGUEL) CONWAY, BVM
Teaching assignments followed—from Nebraska to Iowa to California—but another call was stirring. Inspired by Cardinal Richard Cushing’s appeal for missionaries in Latin America, Miguel met Fr. John Halligan, a Jesuit whose work with street children in Quito, Ecuador, opened a new chapter. Sent by the BVM leadership, Miguel began what became her life’s work.
For 50 years, she served as “Madre” to generations of children and families at the Centro del Muchacho Trabajador—the Working Boys’ Center—which Miguel describes as “a family of families.” More recently, she has helped guide the Fundación Familias Trabajadoras—Working Families Foundation—a ministry founded by former program participants at Muchacho Trabajador that is based on Gospel values and shared responsibility.
At the heart of Miguel’s vocation is a deep kinship with BVM Foundress Mary Frances Clarke.
“She responded to the call to teach God’s love to the poor and marginalized in a country not her own,” Miguel says. “She is, and always has been, my idol.”
Miguel has lived and worked in Ecuador for nearly 60 years. It is where her heart and her vocation led her.
“Being a BVM means helping people know they are loved,” she says. “And empowering them, supported by that love, to change their lives and circumstances.”

## THERESA MARIE (DOROTHY) GLEESON, BVM
Theresa Gleeson, BVM has spent seven decades living a vocation she recognized almost before she had words for it.
“I knew,” she says. “From a very young age, I knew that’s what I was being called to do—and I wanted to do it.”
**Born Into Hardship, Formed by Faith**
Born in 1937 during the Great Depression, Theresa was the fifth of seven children in an Irish Catholic family. Living in Pennsylvania, her parents, William and Dorothea, were forced to sell the family butcher shop and their home. Theresa’s mother was pregnant with her at the time.
“They lost everything,” Theresa recalls.
Aunt Doll, Theresa’s paternal aunt, lived in Glendale, Calif. She and her husband were doing well financially, and she invited her brother and his family to move to the west coast.
Once her father was working again and the family was back on their feet, they moved to South Glendale—“the other side of the tracks,” as Theresa calls it—where working-class immigrant families, many of them from Mexico, formed a close-knit community. It was there, at Holy Family Parish, that her life-long relationship with the BVMs began.
**Loving People**
Theresa and her siblings were educated by the BVMs from grade school through high school.
“They were so good to us,” Theresa says. “Their kindness and understanding were amazing. They were just loving people.”
Her faith deepened after her mother died suddenly of a heart attack when Theresa was just fourteen. Her father, whom she describes as “a very religious guy,” never remarried and raised the children on his own.
“My dad was in the Holy Name Society,” she says. “Once a month, he’d get up at six in the morning to go down to Los Angeles for adoration services. One day I said, ‘Dad, can I go with you?’ And he started taking me with him. That just helped me flourish. It fed my soul.”
After graduating from high school, Theresa worked for a year at the telephone company in Glendale to save the money she needed to travel to Dubuque, Iowa, and begin her novitiate.

## THERESA MARIE (DOROTHY) GLEESON, BVM
“My dad was proud to have a child who followed this track,” she says. “But he didn’t have the money to send me halfway across the country.”
One she had her travel money in hand, Theresa entered the congregation without hesitation.
“It wasn’t a difficult decision,” she says.
**A Love for Language and Culture**
Growing up amongst Mexican neighbors influenced Theresa’s worldview and her future ministry.
“They were bilingual and they were so sweet,” she recalls. “I just loved them, their culture, and especially their language.”
She would later earn a bachelor’s degree in Spanish and a master’s degree in Spanish literature, eventually using the language in her missions across the United States, Ecuador, and Ghana.
**Teaching in East L.A.**
One of Theresa’s most beloved missions was teaching fifth grade in East Los Angeles.
“Those children were wonderful,” she says. “Very difficult—but I loved them.”
Speaking Spanish allowed her to connect not only with students, but with their families as well.
“It was great to be able to talk to the parents,” she says.
Decades later, she remains in contact with some of her former students, including one who became a judge.
“He still calls and emails,” she says.
Later in life, Theresa served as a formation director for the BVM Community—a role she found deeply meaningful and challenging dealing with a myriad of personalities and situations.
“Those were the most difficult years,” she admits, but she saw God’s hand in the outcome.
“God is good,” she says. “God is faithful. It all worked out.”
**With a Snap of the Fingers**
Looking back, Theresa says her years with the BVMs feel brief.
“It went just like that,” she says, snapping her fingers. “I loved what I was doing. I loved who I was. And I loved the BVM Community.”
Her faith remains rooted in a simple conviction:“I believe there’s a plan for each of us,” she says.
For Theresa, that plan unfolded in a life dedicated to service, language, and love.

## BRIGID MARY HART, BVM
Growing up in Milwaukee, Brigid Mary Hart, BVM did not see herself as particularly “Irish,” even though her family roots traced directly to Ireland. As a second-generation Irish American, she remembers the culture around her differently from friends of hers whose families had immigrated more recently.
“We were American,” Brigid Mary says. “It was no big deal about being Irish.”
**A Milwaukee Childhood**
The neighborhood where she grew up was driven more by religion and culture than by ethnicity.
“We lived in an upper-class neighborhood that was really Jewish and Catholic,” she recalls.
Yet even as a child, Brigid Mary was quietly absorbing lessons about the broader world. She later reflected on memories she did not fully understand at the time—like seeing Black domestic workers, acutely aware of unwritten “sundown” rules, hurriedly getting to the bus stop so they could get home before dark.
“You begin to think about class and about some of the hidden prejudices that were part of the culture,” she says.
Those reflections would become part of Brigid Mary’s lifelong awareness as she began her vocation.
**A Vocation That Wouldn’t Go Away**
Brigid Mary attended Holy Angels Academy, where the joyful presence of the sisters left a deep impression.
The example of the sisters she encountered as a student struck a chord. She noticed not only their commitment to their work, but the balance they seemed to live.
“They enjoyed being with the students,” Brigid Mary recalls. “But they also liked going home for prayer and being with their community.”
Still, religious life was not part of her carefully planned future. In fact, Brigid Mary had already enrolled at Clarke University in Dubuque, Iowa, and was looking forward to campus life.
Then, rather unexpectedly, she thought that perhaps somebody was trying to tell her something.
“I needed to get God off my back,” she says with a laugh. “So I came to Mount Carmel for a few weeks. And I never left.”
**Expanding Horizons**
Like many BVM sisters, Brigid Mary began her ministry in education, but traditional classroom teaching was not where her greatest passion lay.She began exploring other possibilities within education. That search eventually led her to Montessori training—a discovery that changed the course of her ministry.

## BRIGID MARY HART, BVM
“Montessori was my favorite ministry,” she says. “Creating the environment for learning, that was something I really loved.”
She found joy in designing classrooms that encouraged curiosity and independence. Watching children become absorbed in their work was one of the most rewarding parts of the ministry.
“They were delightful,” she says of her students. “Especially when they would get involved and get lost in their world. Concentration took over.”
Brigid Mary taught in Iowa and New York before going to Colorado, where she spent nearly 30 years. She served in parish schools, parish ministry, and in Montessori classrooms.
Those years also broadened her experience in ways she never expected. Opportunities for travel and study enriched both her faith and her understanding of the wider world.
“There were chances to do things I might never have done otherwise,” she says.
She participated in a study trip that included time in Rome and two weeks in Israel, and she has also spent time in the Philippines and the West Indies.
“You meet different people and experience different cultures,” she says. “Those experiences give you perspective and add a lot of richness to your life.”
**A Life of Faith and Openness**
Brigid Mary eventually returned to the Midwest, spending 15 years in Chicago working in a variety of ministries. At Wright Hall, a senior residence for the BVM Community, she served as activities director. She also worked in ESL programs, parish ministry, and assisting the Cenacle Community of women religious.
Throughout her years of ministry, Brigid Mary often followed her curious nature. Her willingness to sometimes step into the unknown allowed her to grow, learn, and remain energized in her work. She embraced each new chapter with openness, thankful for the opportunities to explore her interests and find her passions.
Today in retirement, she continues to explore—especially reading and art. She has taken icon writing workshops and enjoys creative expression, even if she modestly says her work is “dabbling.”
Looking back, Brigid Mary doesn’t describe her vocation as a dramatic calling. Instead, guided by faith and curiosity, it unfolded step by step with that decision to, as she jokingly says, “get God off my back.”

## KATHERINE “KATE” (ST. WILMA) KEATING, BVM
Katherine “Kate” Keating, BVM is very straightforward about her life and her vocation: “I’ve not disliked it ever. And I had a good time—most of the time.”
**Windy Cindy Roots**
Chicago born and bred, Kate grew up in Humboldt Park on the city’s west side—a neighborhood of immigrant faith and fierce parish loyalty. Our Lady of the Angels was her family’s parish and school. It was close enough to Kate’s house that she walked home for lunch every day.
Her father William, who died when Kate was in high school, had grown up in the same church, making her and her older brother second-generation parishioners. For Kate, faith was woven into daily life with devotion and humor.
“There were three churches in the neighborhood,” Kate remembers. “The Polish church, the Slovak church, and Our Lady of the Angels.”
Kate’s mother, Sarah, who played the organ and sang in the choir, often went to the Polish church for confession.
“The priest didn’t speak English,” Kate explains. “She would say, ‘I can go to confession, and he won’t understand anything.’”
The story still makes her laugh.
When the devastating Our Lady of the Angels fire occurred in 1958, Kate was two years into her novitiate in Dubuque, Iowa.
“My mother still lived in the parish,” she recalls. “We knew families. We knew kids.”
**From the Diamond to the Motherhouse**
Kate began her BVM journey in 1956 at age 18. But it was not necessarily her first choice at the time. A gifted baseball player, she announced to her mother that she was going to join the Bloomer Girls, a professional women’s team.
“My mother said, ‘Over my dead body,’” Kate laughs. “So I said, ‘Then maybe I’ll join the BVMs.’ That made her happy.”
Behind Kate’s humor was a call nurtured by 12 years of BVM education, and especially by one teacher.
“There was always a favorite nun,” Kate says. “Mine was Sister Paula Kelly. She taught biology. I hated biology, but I loved her.”
**Good Trouble**
BVM life wasn’t always a perfect fit for a young woman who loved baseball, noise, and jokes.

## KATHERINE “KATE” (ST. WILMA) KEATING, BVM
“I broke all the rules,” she admits.
Silent Sundays were difficult for Kate. Playing baseball on the lawn in front of the Mother General’s office in full habit earned a reprimand.
Still, Kate says, “They kept me.”
**Jokes and Tough Streets**
Kate earned a degree in mathematics and spent many years teaching. She particularly enjoyed junior high students.
“They say junior high kids are tough,” she recalls. “But I really liked them. They were good. I’d give them two extra points on tests if they told me a joke. That helped some kids pass.”
Her ministries carried her across Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, and Montana. In Lincoln, Neb., she started a girls’ softball team using Chicago’s unique 16-inch ball.
“I carried that ball in the trunk of my car all the time,” she says. “People had never seen anything like it.”
After earning a master’s degree in education administration, Kate spent five demanding years as the principal of St. Joseph School in Chicago’s Cabrini-Green neighborhood.
“It was rough,” she says. “But you went to those buildings. You walked up the stairs. You showed up. You talked to the parents.”
Kate knew that immersion in community life was important for the success of her students.
**A Life Lived Fully**
In retirement, Kate’s spirituality deepened through hospice ministry. For 10 years, she sat with the dying so others could rest.
“That was a very moving experience,” she says. “It was a marvelous experience.”
One night, she and other hospice workers sang to a dying woman from Ireland who requested songs from her childhood.
“She was so grateful,” Kate recalls. “It was like prayer.”
Her love for Chicago remains as strong as ever. A lifelong sports fan, she and her good friend, Dorothy Gaffney, BVM drove to Wrigley Field from Dubuque after the Cubs won the 2016 World Series to soak in the atmosphere of the victory parade.
Today, Kate stays active in Schola and enjoys the company of her BVM sisters. When looking back on her missions, she notes that they were “97.2% wonderful and 2.8% ugh.”

## KATHERINE “KATE” (ST. WILMA) KEATING, BVM
Kate intentionally chooses community life: “I like the doors open. I like hearing people.”
As for what 70 years as a BVM means, she answers simply: “I’ve had a good life. I’ve met good people. And I’ve never been sorry.”

#### Messiah Z. Nantwi
March 8, 2002 ~ March 1, 2025
It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Messiah Z. Nantwi, who was born on March 8, 2002, and left this world unexpectedly on March 1, 2025. Messiah was a beloved son, cherished brother, and a brilliant young mind who touched the lives of many.
He is survived by his devoted father, Patterson, and his loving mother, Leslie. Messiah was preceded in death by his beloved sister Ahjani Akira Nantwi, who passed away two years ago, leaving a void in the hearts of those who knew them both.

#### Delores Marie White
January 8, 1942 ~ March 2, 2025
Delores Marie White was graciously gifted by God on January 8, 1942. Delores, the youngest of six children, was born in Pittsburgh, PA to parents Ms. Willie Lou Prophet and Mr. Willie Benjamin White. At the very early age of two years old, both of Delores’ parents passed away suddenly due to Tuberculosis. No longer having the care and guidance of her loving parents she was raised by her paternal grandmother, Ms. Sally Shavers in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
She attended Fourth Street Elementary School as well as Lee Elementary School.

#### Lillian Mae Cain
May 6, 1928 ~ February 26, 2025
Mrs. Lillian Mae (Burton) Cain was born in Gumberry, North Carolina on May 6, 1928. She was the 2nd of three children born to the late Paul Burton and Eunice Kee. Gumberry, North Carolina was where she met and married her first husband Chauncey Belle at a very young age and bore two sons, Burton Richard Belle and John Paul Belle.
Lillian was a woman of remarkable strength and determination. Living life on her own terms. She was known for her no-nonsense attitude and straightforward approach to life, qualities that endeared her to many.

#### Claude Brewer Peterson
May 27, 1939 ~ February 27, 2025
Claude Brewer Peterson was a loving husband, father, grandfather, brother, uncle and cousin. A self-made man, he worked tirelessly to put himself through college, ultimately becoming a research chemist who shied away from recognition but loved his work and being in the lab. Passionate about advancing science, he created three patents with the U.S. Patent and Trade Office, while also authoring academic articles based on his discoveries.
Born to Evelyn and Roland Peterson on May 27, 1939, at Harlem Hospital in New York City Claude married and raised two sons, Keith and Dwight.

#### Freddie Sylvester Brooks
February 15, 1960 ~ February 17, 2025
You may have known him as that smart, knowledgeable and engaging CEO of Binding Products, Inc., a successful business where customers came first and who deeply cared about the awesome staff who worked for him. Or, maybe you remember that nice man who was a volunteer coach for a little league basketball team. Maybe you were a neighbor, friend or coworker whose heart was warmed as Freddie proudly and lovingly shared stories about his beautiful children. Our family knows him by his broad smile, deep insights, great sense of humor; and as a loving father, son, brother and friend.

#### Neil Cedric Dingle, Sr.
August 2, 1948 ~ February 13, 2025
Neil Cedric Dingle was born on August 2, 1948 to Kermit Theodore Dingle and Vivian Barry Dingle in Harlem Hospital in Manhattan, but was raised in The Bronx.
Growing up, Neil was very athletic. He was very good at whatever sport he was competing in, especially basketball, handball, and paddleball. He was also in a bowling league for ten years. He was a very pleasant person to be around with a good sense of humor.
After graduating from William Howard Taft High School, he enlisted in the United States Air Force in 1966.

#### Wayne A. Williams
March 3, 1958 ~ January 20, 2025
Wayne Anthony Williams was born on May 3, 1958 to the late Sylvia Williams and Willie Govan. Wayne was the middle child of 3 boys. He was raised with his brothers in Bamberg, South Carolina until the age of seven when his mother relocated him and his two brothers to New York City in 1966.
Wayne completed his education in the New York Public School System. After High School, Wayne served in the US Army for a short time. Wayne was a jack of all trades who worked various jobs to provide for his family and help others. Wayne met Karen Smith in 1990.

#### Hermann Fulbert Touvoli
April 10, 1973 ~ January 30, 2025
For he was
An immovable object—committed, principled, and chiseled by life’s lessons.
And just as well, an unstoppable force—unrelenting, fearless, and imbued with relentless vigor.
Calculated yet unbounded; He stood as a pillar of authenticity. He retained complete faith in his internal worth. We hope he now sees that he is also worthy of rest because his legacy is imprinted on everyone gathered in this room today.

#### Bettie Ruth Ward
September 15, 1923 ~ February 7, 2025
Bettie Ruth Ward was born in Mississippi on September 15th to the late Edith Gill and Jeff Darby. At a young age Bettie accepted Christ as her personal Lord and Savior.
As a young woman, Bettie met Jeffrey Ward and they married on November 29, 1953.
Bettie worked as a dietary aide at Jacoby Medical Center. After 30 years of faithful service she retired.
Bettie leaves to cherish her memories: her children, sister-in-law, nieces, nephews, grandchildren, and a host of other relatives and friends.

#### Yvonne Elaine Dixon
December 22, 1943 ~ January 28, 2025
YVONNE ELAINE DIXON was the tenth and youngest child born to Madge and William Dicks. She was born on December 22, 1943 in the village of Harlem, New York. All of her nine siblings preceded her in death when she left this earthly life on Tuesday, January 28, 2025 at the age of 81.
Yvonne attended elementary and junior high schools in Manhattan, and graduated from Jane Adams Vocational High School in the Bronx.

#### Pamela Conner
January16, 1973 ~ January 22, 2025
Pamela Conner, age 52, passed away peacefully on Wednesday, January 22, 2025 at Calvary Hospital surrounded by loved ones. Pamela was born on January 16, 1973 in Bronx, New York to the late Hannah Toney and Walter Conner. She was the youngest of their five children.
Pamela spent most her life in the Bronx where she planted roots, formed bonds and developed lifelong friendships. She attended Roosevelt High School in the Bronx, and later went on to pursue both a degree in Computer Science and Criminal Justice.

#### Helen Elizabeth Johnson
August 15, 1964 ~ January 22, 2025
Helen Elizabeth Johnson, lovingly known as “Big Mama,” was born on August 15, 1964, in Harlem, New York, to her proud parents, James Abel and Dolores Larcus. The youngest of six children, Helen carried a bright spirit and a heart full of love throughout her life.
Helen’s educational journey began at P.S. 46, followed by I.S. 10 for middle school, and she later graduated from Martin Luther King High School. Her passion for learning led her to Touro College, where she earned her Associate’s degree in 1999. Determined to further her education, she went on to achieve her Bachelor’s degree in Human Services in 2001.

#### Joan Deloris Thomas
July 19, 1933 ~ January 18, 2025
Joan Deloris (Lewis) Thomas born July 19, 1933 to Clifton Lawrence Sr. and Matoka Lewis in Marion County, South Carolina. The family then migrated to NYC where Clifton Lewis II (Junior) was born. They settled in Harlem (Sugar Hill). Joan attended public schools, graduated from George Washington HS then shortly attended college in Virginia. During her formative years Joan enjoyed life to the fullest – being with her friends, enjoying people and having a good time. An “uptown girl” who truly loved her home town, Harlem, and represented a time of Renaissance where Harlem was a place of sophistication, style, grace and Black pride. She loved her community.

#### Steven Frank Bailey
April 5, 1946 ~ January 6, 2025
Steven Frank Bailey: Born to Blanche Beatrice Bailey and Louis Bailey, at Lincoln Hospital, Bronx, New York, on April 5, 1946. The third child, and sibling to Michael Louis Bailey, and Jacqueline Mary Bailey. Later, there was another addition to the family, Stephanie.
Steven, a Bronx native who attended both elementary and high school in the borough, enlisted in the Marine Corps at the age of 17. This decision sparked a conflict with his mother, who strongly opposed his choice. His father, however, supported his ambition.

#### Gloria Princella Blanchard
October 13, 1943 ~ January 7, 2025
Gloria Princella Blanchard was born in New York City, to the proud parents of Edgar Stover and Princella Phillips on October 13th, 1943. At 81 years old, she was the youngest of their two children. After high school, she dedicated her career to the New York City Blood Center as a technician. She was a faithful and long-term member of St. Charles Church and a proud member of the Order of the Eastern Star.
She leaves to mourn her passing: her brother Winfred Phillips and beloved sister Debra (Kim), and her children Princella, Milton, Dorlisa (Calvin Palmer), Michael (Sheila Stover), & Bryette.

#### Yvonne Eva Smith
July 18, 1944 ~ January 2, 2025
Yvonne Eva Smith, born Eva Yvonne Nelson on July 18, 1944 in New York City to Dorothy Miller and Henry Nelson. Yvonne graduated from Central Commercial High School in 1962 where she majored in Merchandising in Midtown Manhattan.
On June 15, 1966, she married Larry Smith and the following November 27th , they welcomed their daughter Brandi Belinda Smith into the world.
Yvonne worked at the Post Office in her early 20’s and then went on to work for the Internal Revenue Service where she retired.

#### Bernard Eric Hewitt
August 8, 1995 ~ December 14, 2024
We gather here today to celebrate the life of Bernard Eric Hewitt, Son of Andrea Johnson and the late Garfield Bernard. Bernard was a man whose light brightened the lives of everyone who knew him. Bernard was born on August 8, 1995, in Manhattan, at New York Presbyterian Hospital. the vibrant heart of the city, attending Public School 28, I.S. 164, and Brandeis High School in Manhattan. Bernard’s dedication to learning led him to Bronx Community College, where he earned a degree in Business Administration and Social Work.

#### Manuel Calixto Aviles
November 5, 1922 ~ December 26, 2024
Our beloved Father, Husband, Grandfather, Great-Grandfather, Brother, Uncle and Friend was called home on Thursday, December 26, 2024.
He was born to the late Manuel Aviles Ortiz and Monserrate Aponte De Aviles in Coamo, Puerto Rico, USA. He was the middle eldest of 11 children. He worked at a private school, Ethical Culture Fieldston School in Manhattan, as a maintenance worker. Manuel Calixto was very active in doing community work and volunteered his services. He earned the respect of every one in our community. In his late 50s, a brave accomplishment, he went back to school to earn his GED.

#### Stephanie Anita Dodds-Sydnor
May 7, 1948 ~ December 20, 2024
Stephanie Anita Dodds was born on May 7, 1948 to Doris Beckman Dodds and Thomas Jefferson Dodds. She passed on December 20, 2024. She had 5 siblings, Roxanne Dodds, Erica A. Dodds and Donna M. Dodds. Her brothers David Dodds and Thomas Dodds, Jr. preceded her in death. Stephanie graduated from Brandeis High School. She worked as a Nurse's Assistant at the Flower Fifth Avenue Hospital for a few years. Later she was employed at the prestigious law firms of F. Lee Bailey and Aaron J. Broder, where she was an office manager and deposition clerk. Always studious, and driven, she graduated from the College of New Rochelle Rosa Parks Campus, on May 29, 1994, where she received her bachelor's degree

#### Barbara Alston Fuller
March 11, 1939 ~ November 24, 2024
Barbara Alston Fuller, born at Harlem Hospital to parents Nathaniel “Nat” Fuller and Dorothy Louise Alston, grew to become a performer whose artistic career panned Broadway, television, and film. She left an indelible mark on the entertainment industry and the hearts of those she loved. Her journey, marked by resilience, creativity, and compassion, was extraordinary both on and off the stage.
Barbara’s life in show business was remarkable. Barbara also appeared in the play The Wedding Band (1972), a powerful work that explored relationships and human connection.

#### Shirley Jean Woods
May 30, 1941 ~ December 4, 2024
Devout Christian, Loving Mother, and Loyal Friend, Shirley J. Woods, God’s gift, was born in Sarasota, Florida, on May 30, 1941, to the late Leroy Woods and Mabel McElvy. Up to the age of 14, she was raised by her maternal grandparents, King & Nettie McElvy.
In 1955, Shirley accompanied her mother when she relocated from Quincy, FL. to Harlem NY, in pursuit of new opportunities. She achieved a personal milestone by completing her high school education, a testament to her resilience and commitment to self-improvement.

#### Garnett S. Lewis
August 3, 1945 ~ December 8, 2024
Garnett Sylvester Lewis was born in Jamaica, WI, and raised in Bellas Gate, St. Catherine on August 3, 1945. _Jeremiah 1:5_ states “before he was formed in his mother’s womb God knew him and called him to be.” This comforts us to know he is God’s. He was the third of eight children born to Naomi and Henry Lewis. While in Bellas Gate he met his beloved wife Iris Blake-Lewis and together they have five beautiful children Devon Lewis, Marcia Lewis, Wayne Lewis, Jacqueline Lewis, Nadene Lewis. They both migrated to America for a better life for their family. They settled in New York City in the late 70’s, in the borough of Manhattan where he resided until his passing.

#### Esther Mae Middleton
February 1, 1942 ~ December 5, 2024
Esther "Pate” Middleton graced her parents Osborne and Ethel Hicks, and the world, with her presence on February 1, 1942, in Alexander City, Alabama. Esther peacefully chose to rest in her longtime home of Harlem, New York on December 5, 2024.
Pate, as she was affectionately called, was united in holy matrimony with the late Clinton Maynard Middleton. Upon migrating from Alabama, she found success in New York City through 30 years of employment within the telephone company Bell Atlantic, known more recently as Verizon. She was a devoted mother, sister, friend, and longtime member of Union Baptist Church as an Auxiliary Usher.

#### Lincoln Beresford Harris
August 30, 1951 ~ November 11, 2024
Lincoln Beresford Harris was born on August 30, 1951, to the happy parents who preceded him, Beresford, and Joyce Harris, of Eden Vale, St. James, Jamaica. He was the sixth of thirteen children; two younger brothers preceded him. God called Lincoln home on Monday, November 11, 2024.
His education began at Goodwill Elementary School, then went on to Harrison Memorial High School in Montego Bay, Jamaica. Lincoln was an excellent student and excelled in academics which led him upon graduation to work in the Hotel Industry.

**Composer, poet, musician, writer**

Few women composers and writers could create in a lifetime what Regina Harris Baiocchi has composed in the first 45 years of her life. Her abilities are so multi-faceted that whether she is composing for piano, drums, or clarinet, or for voice, or for any of the other instruments, with which she can work, or whether writing novels, her newest effort, Baiocchi’s works easily find an appreciative audience. For the many individuals and groups who have commissioned her works, Baiocchi’s creativity has appeared to be in endless supply.

## Started Writing Early
Regina Harris Baiocchi was born on July 16, 1956, in Chicago, Illinois, to Elgie Harris Jr. and Lanzie Mozelle Belmont Harris. Baiocchi grew up in a large household in the housing projects of Chicago’s south side. As the third of eight surviving children born to the Harris family, she was raised in a home where, as a child, she was exposed to music, art, and books. At one time, her father had attended college, where he studied creative writing, although he never completed a degree. He was a truck driver, writer, visual artist, and an ordained church deacon. In addition to these activities, he played the harmonica and the fiddle. Baiocchi’s mother was a teacher before she left teaching to raise her family. As a small child, Baiocchi attended Burnside and Hardigan elementary schools. With the family’s conversion to Catholicism, Baiocchi transferred to St. Elizabeth’s Elementary School. She began singing in her church choir at age four and with her mother’s encouragement, Baiocchi began writing songs, even before she began her formal study of music at age nine, with guitar lessons. Age nine is also when she began to sing in the school choir and the Girl’s Choir, a community ensemble.
In 1970 Baiocchi attended St. Mary Springs Academy in Fond de Lac, Wisconsin. Then, in 1971, Baiocchi transferred to Richards Vocational High School in Chicago, where she began studying the recorder. Neither high school was a good fit, and so in 1971, she transferred to Paul Lawrence Dunbar Vocational High School and continued her music education by studying counterpoint, theory, arranging, and composition. She also sang in the chorus and played trumpet, French horn, and coronet in several of the school bands. The environment at Paul Lawrence was a nurturing one for

### At a Glance …
Born on July 16, 1956, in Chicago, IL; married Gregory Baiocchi, July 12, 1975. _Education:_ Roosevelt University, BM, 1978; coursework at Illinois Institute of Technology, 1984–86; coursework at Northwest University. 1990–92; New York University, certificate in public relations, 1991; De Paul University, MM, 1995.
**Career:** Composer, numerous pieces for instrument and voice, 1978–; Dunbar Vocational High School, teacher, 1979; St Bride’s Junior High School, teacher, 1979–81; St Thomas the Apostle Junior High School, teacher, 1982–1986; poet, 1980s–; Telaction Corporation, audio quality control analyst and writer, 1986–89; Catholic Theological Union in Chicago, public relations director, 1989–94; Steppenwolf Theater, composer and director, 1997; Ravinia Music Festival Music Illumination Program, artistic director, 1997–99; East-West University, lecturer, 2000–; novelist, 2003–.
**Selected awards:** Poets and Patrons Award for Poetry for “Teeter Totter,” and “Ghetto Child,” 1980s; McDonald’s Literary Achievement Award, for “Mama’s Will,” 1988; Illinois Arts Council grant, 1995; Chicago Music Association award, 1995; Art Institute of Chicago grant for _Gbeldahoven: No One’s Child_, 1997; National Endowment for the Arts Regional Artists Program grant _African Hands_, 1997.
**Addresses:**_Home_—40 East 9th Street, 1816, Chicago, IL, 60605. _Office—_ English and Communications Department, East-West University, 816 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago, IL, 60605.

## Started Writing Early
### At a Glance …
a fledgling composer like Baiocchi. In an on-line interview for the _Web Institute for Teachers_, Baoicchi told interviewer Julieanna Richardson that she “would write something on Monday and [on] Wednesday I would hear it. And the teachers made sure that the students played it the way they played Beethoven or Bach or some of the other marching band stuff we did.”
Baiocchi was only 14 years old when she met Gregory Baiocchi, a 15-year-old Italian-American boy from Chicago’s north side. In spite of the differences in their family background, the couple forged a close relationship. In a 2002 biographical entry about Baiocchi’s life for her book, _From Spirituals to Symphonies: African-American Women Composers and their Music_, Helen Walker-Hill recounted an episode that demonstrated how vast those differences really were. On one visit to see the teen-age Baiocchi, Gregory entered the projects and was accosted and robbed. At one point he was held by his feet and dangled over the edge of a high rise building. Walker-Hill related that it was “only when the girlfriend of one of the gang members recognized him” that the teen-ager was released. Soon after, the Harris family moved out of the projects and into a home in a safer area of town. Baiocchi graduated from high school in 1974 and the following year, she married Gregory Baiocchi on July 12, 1975.

## Began Training as a Composer
In the fall of 1975, Baiocchi enrolled at Roosevelt University’s Chicago Music College. At Roosevelt she continued her studies in composition and theory and began studying the piano, but as she explained in an interview with _Contemporary Black Biography (CBB)_, Baiocchi did not find college to be as nurturing an environment as high school had been. Not only was she the only African-American student in the composition and theory department, she was also the only female. Baiocchi had a talent and an interest in writing pop music, jazz, blues, and gospel, but the emphasis in her classes was exclusively on classical music. When she tried to compose other styles of music, “a lot of times it was rejected as ‘pop shit.’” She explained to _CBB_ that “I was rudely reminded that they were teaching me to write classical music.” In spite of these difficulties, Baiocchi completed a bachelor of music degree in 1978, with a major in composition and theory. Her senior recital included several new works, including _Chas é For Wind Sextet_ and a string quartet _Realizations_. Baiocchi stayed at Roosevelt and spent a year of continued studies in the graduate program, where she composed her first published work, _Two Piano Etudes_.
Video 5  
Video Muted
After college, Baiocchi began working in the first of several teaching jobs. Her father’s connections at church led to a summer job at Dunbar High School teaching theory. This job was followed by two years at St. Bride’s Junior High School, where she taught mathematics. Her next teaching job was at St. Thomas the Apostle Junior High School, where she taught mathematics and social studies. During her tenure as a teacher, she also wrote poetry. Two of her poems, “Teeter Totter,” which was published in the _Chicago Tribune_ Magazine and “Ghetto Child,” received a Poets & Patrons Award for Poetry. Baiocchi was herself a student during her last two years at St. Thomas. In 1984 she enrolled at the Illinois Institute of Design, where she studied visual and project design. At the same time, she studied calligraphy privately with an artist friend, a practice most obviously seen in her own handwritten music scores.

## Began Training as a Composer
After she left St. Thomas in 1986, Baiocchi moved her career into another direction with a new job, first as an audio quality control analyst, then as a writer for three years at Telaction Corporation. Even while working, she was busy as a choir director and composing music, including _Father, We Thank You_. Baiocchi also turned her talents toward creative writing, with a short story, “Mama’s Will,” which won a McDonald’s Literary Achievement Award in 1988 and was read aloud at the Douglas Fairbanks Theater in New York City. The following year, she composed _Two Zora Neale Hurston Songs_, which were based on one of Hurston’s essays. At about that same time, Baiocchi was preparing to make another career change. In 1989 she began a new career with a job in public relations. In a personal reflection essay written for William C. Banfield’s, _Musical Landscapes in Color: Conversations with Black Composers_, Baiocchi explained that she initially chose public relations “just because there are no jobs in music.” With the move away from teaching, she was also able to find more time for composing music. As an added benefit of her new job, she gained the experience and means to promote her own music.

## Public Relations Benefited Career
As the public relations director for the Catholic Theological Union in Chicago, Baiocchi was busy with the organization’s newsletters and media releases, as well as setting up public events. In addition to her demanding job, Baiocchi took on new responsibilities when she enrolled at Northwestern University in 1990 and began studying public relations. During this period of time she composed _Miles per Hour_, which premiered at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra on May 19, 1990, and _We Real Cool_ Baiocchi next completed a certificate in public relations at New York University in 1991. To add to her already full life, Baiocchi agreed to become composer-in-residence for Mostly Music, an organization that sponsored children’s music programs and concerts.
Although she was clearly busy with work, school, and her music, Baiocchi found that the combination of these activities worked well with her own talents. In an interview with Walker-Hill, Baiocchi discussed this blending of public relations and music: “I don’t know why [music schools] don’t have a promotional curriculum in conjunction with any sort of arts degree musicians can’t just sit and practice and expect to have an audience.” With her experience in public relations and her schooling in that field, Baiocchi was able to design and promote her own concerts. She scheduled the first of these concerts during the fall of 1991 and used it as a forum to introduce her newest compositions. She also composed three new works during that time, _Autumn Night, Foster Pet_, and _Crystal Stair_.

## Public Relations Benefited Career
Within a short time, Baiocchi was holding concerts in both fall and spring, as she continued to compose and present new works. She also discovered that her efforts to combine music and public relations were becoming very successful. She began receiving invitations to become a guest lecturer and composer at several universities, and most importantly, she received commissions to create and present her music for several different venues. In 1991 she composed her first work for orchestra, _Orchestra Suite_, which premiered at the Detroit Symphony Orchestra in February of 1992. As composer-in-residence for Mostly Music, Baiocchi wrote _Shadows_ and _Legacy_, both of which were vocal and instrumental compositions, and _A Few Black Voices_, a rap. Also in 1992, she composed a piece for a four-act ballet, _Bwana’s Libation_, and an additional composition _Sketches For Piano Trio_, which was commissioned by St. Mary’s Episcopal Church in Philadelphia. In addition to composing these works, Baiocchi conducted music composition workshops and guest lectured at several colleges, including Northwestern University, Wayne State University, and Columbia College during 1993.

## Talents Recognized
Beginning in 1993 and continuing for the next several years, Baiocchi received grants to help support her work from the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs. She composed three new works during 1993: _Mason Room, Much In Common_, and _Ain’t Nobody’s Child_. Soon afterward, during 1994, Baiocchi decided to leave the Catholic Theological Union and begin work on a master’s degree in music composition at De Paul University. In February of that year, she was the featured composer in a concert sponsored by the American Women Composers/Midwest at the Harold Washington Library. Some of her newest compositions were featured at performances during 1994, including _Teddy Bear Suite_, which was performed by the Pennsylvania Youth Orchestra. Another new piece, _QFX_, was performed by the Milwaukee Brass Quintet at the University of Wisconsin campus in Milwaukee.
Without the demands of her job at the Catholic Theological Union, Baiocchi’s creative output soared, and she composed several new pieces, including _Liszten, My Husband Is Not a Hat_, for which Baiocchi received a grant from AT&T, and _Three Pieces For Greg_, a short composition for orchestra. Before 1994 ended, Baiocchi had completed several additional works, including _Deborah, Best Friends, Ancestor’s Medley, Much In Common, After The Rain_, and _Say No To Guns_. By this time in her career, Baiocchi had proven to have a great versatility of talent. She was composing for a wide selection of instruments and performance formats, including voice and dance. In the space of 15 years, she had composed works for clarinet sextet, string quartet, trumpet solo, cello, jazz ensemble, and piano. She had also written songs, a ballet, and orchestra compositions.

## Talents Recognized
Baiocchi completed her master of music degree at De Paul University in 1995. Of course, as was the case in the past, her studies did not end with the granting of another degree. She next began studying jazz piano with Alan Swain, a jazz musician and music professor at De Paul. Most importantly for Baiocchi, she also began to study composition with Hale Smith, a classical and jazz composer. Her study with Smith was especially important to Baiocchi’s growth as a holistic composer. In her interview with _CBB_, Baiocchi credited much of her success to her mentor Hale Smith, with whom she began studying in 1995.
1995 was also a year in which Baiocchi received a grant from the Illinois Arts Council to develop children’s programs; as well as a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts Regional Artists Program. That same year she received a Chicago Music Association award. Even though she was once again invited to Columbia College and Northwestern University as a guest lecturer and composer, Baiocchi still found time to compose lyrics for an orchestra work that featured soprano, _Good News Falls Gently_, at the Musicali di Musica Sacra in Rome. She also composed two additional new pieces, _Darry’s Rose_ and _Friday Night_.

## Accumulated an Oeuvre of Work
During 1996 Baiocchi appeared as a guest lecturer and composer at Northwestern University and Indiana University. During 1996 and into 1997, Baiocchi completed two dramatic works. The first was a one-act play with incidental music, _Dreamhoppers_. Her first opera, _Gbeldahoven: No One’s Child_, about Zora Neale Hurston and Langston Hughes, was a composition that spawned from the 1993 Hurston songs and the composer’s original libretto. _Gbeldahoven: No One’s Child_ received funding from the Art Institute of Chicago and the Lila Wallace/Reader’s Digest Fund. This opera reflected the compilation of all that Baiocchi had learned about music during the previous 20 years. In her 2000 interview with Richardson, Baiocchi said that when she looked at this opera, she was able to see “where just about everything I’ve ever done in my life appeared in that opera in more ways than any other musical piece that I’ve written.” Although her opera has not yet been mounted with a full orchestra, it has been performed with piano, cello, and some percussion.

## MIGUEL (MARY MIGUEL) CONWAY, BVM
Miguel Conway, BVM often says she learned community before she could name it.
“I am the third of eight Conway children,” she says. “Four girls, four boys. We all had the experience of a close-knit community from infancy.”
**Rooted in Family and Faith**
Growing up in Boone, Iowa, during the years surrounding World War II meant learning responsibility early. When her father, William, went to war, Miguel and her siblings grew up fast with the help of a strong mother who emphasized faith and family.
That faith was nurtured in classrooms staffed by the BVMs. Miguel’s mother, Kathryn, herself educated by the BVMs, was convinced that they were “the best educators in the world,” Miguel says.
**Faith, Music, and Laughter**
In Boone, a largely non-Catholic town, the sisters’ presence offered both academic rigor and ecumenical openness with the town’s residents.
“The BVM Sisters were known and loved in the community by everybody,” Miguel remembers.
Two teachers left a lasting mark: Sister Mary Leonilda Kerrigan and Sister Mary Gregory Berchmans.
“They taught us to trust in God, to pray, to think, to calculate, and to challenge the issues of our day,” Miguel says.
Music, laughter, and faith filled the Conway home. Miguel and her sisters Pat and Judy became known as “The Conway Trio,” singing and playing instruments at church. They attended daily Mass, and the family gathered weekly to watch Bishop Fulton Sheen on the household’s first television.
After high school, college was the natural next step. Miguel headed off to Clarke University in Dubuque, Iowa, to study math and education.
**A Call That Couldn’t Wait**
A family tragedy sharpened her sense of urgency to begin her vocation. After her brother Mick was killed in an auto accident, Miguel felt she couldn’t ignore it any longer.
“I began to think that it isn’t a good idea to put important things off,” she says. “I knew, even then, that God was calling me to religious life.”
She entered the BVM Community supported wholeheartedly by her parents.
**A Family of Families in Ecuador**
texts.3:
## MIGUEL (MARY MIGUEL) CONWAY, BVM
Teaching assignments followed—from Nebraska to Iowa to California—but another call was stirring. Inspired by Cardinal Richard Cushing’s appeal for missionaries in Latin America, Miguel met Fr. John Halligan, a Jesuit whose work with street children in Quito, Ecuador, opened a new chapter. Sent by the BVM leadership, Miguel began what became her life’s work.
For 50 years, she served as “Madre” to generations of children and families at the Centro del Muchacho Trabajador—the Working Boys’ Center—which Miguel describes as “a family of families.” More recently, she has helped guide the Fundación Familias Trabajadoras—Working Families Foundation—a ministry founded by former program participants at Muchacho Trabajador that is based on Gospel values and shared responsibility.
At the heart of Miguel’s vocation is a deep kinship with BVM Foundress Mary Frances Clarke.
“She responded to the call to teach God’s love to the poor and marginalized in a country not her own,” Miguel says. “She is, and always has been, my idol.”
Miguel has lived and worked in Ecuador for nearly 60 years. It is where her heart and her vocation led her.
“Being a BVM means helping people know they are loved,” she says. “And empowering them, supported by that love, to change their lives and circumstances.”
texts.4:
## THERESA MARIE (DOROTHY) GLEESON, BVM
Theresa Gleeson, BVM has spent seven decades living a vocation she recognized almost before she had words for it.
“I knew,” she says. “From a very young age, I knew that’s what I was being called to do—and I wanted to do it.”
**Born Into Hardship, Formed by Faith**
Born in 1937 during the Great Depression, Theresa was the fifth of seven children in an Irish Catholic family. Living in Pennsylvania, her parents, William and Dorothea, were forced to sell the family butcher shop and their home. Theresa’s mother was pregnant with her at the time.
“They lost everything,” Theresa recalls.
Aunt Doll, Theresa’s paternal aunt, lived in Glendale, Calif. She and her husband were doing well financially, and she invited her brother and his family to move to the west coast.
Once her father was working again and the family was back on their feet, they moved to South Glendale—“the other side of the tracks,” as Theresa calls it—where working-class immigrant families, many of them from Mexico, formed a close-knit community. It was there, at Holy Family Parish, that her life-long relationship with the BVMs began.
**Loving People**
Theresa and her siblings were educated by the BVMs from grade school through high school.
“They were so good to us,” Theresa says. “Their kindness and understanding were amazing. They were just loving people.”
Her faith deepened after her mother died suddenly of a heart attack when Theresa was just fourteen. Her father, whom she describes as “a very religious guy,” never remarried and raised the children on his own.
“My dad was in the Holy Name Society,” she says. “Once a month, he’d get up at six in the morning to go down to Los Angeles for adoration services. One day I said, ‘Dad, can I go with you?’ And he started taking me with him. That just helped me flourish. It fed my soul.”
After graduating from high school, Theresa worked for a year at the telephone company in Glendale to save the money she needed to travel to Dubuque, Iowa, and begin her novitiate.
texts.5:
## THERESA MARIE (DOROTHY) GLEESON, BVM
“My dad was proud to have a child who followed this track,” she says. “But he didn’t have the money to send me halfway across the country.”
One she had her travel money in hand, Theresa entered the congregation without hesitation.
“It wasn’t a difficult decision,” she says.
**A Love for Language and Culture**
Growing up amongst Mexican neighbors influenced Theresa’s worldview and her future ministry.
“They were bilingual and they were so sweet,” she recalls. “I just loved them, their culture, and especially their language.”
She would later earn a bachelor’s degree in Spanish and a master’s degree in Spanish literature, eventually using the language in her missions across the United States, Ecuador, and Ghana.
**Teaching in East L.A.**
One of Theresa’s most beloved missions was teaching fifth grade in East Los Angeles.
“Those children were wonderful,” she says. “Very difficult—but I loved them.”
Speaking Spanish allowed her to connect not only with students, but with their families as well.
“It was great to be able to talk to the parents,” she says.
Decades later, she remains in contact with some of her former students, including one who became a judge.
“He still calls and emails,” she says.
Later in life, Theresa served as a formation director for the BVM Community—a role she found deeply meaningful and challenging dealing with a myriad of personalities and situations.
“Those were the most difficult years,” she admits, but she saw God’s hand in the outcome.
“God is good,” she says. “God is faithful. It all worked out.”
**With a Snap of the Fingers**
Looking back, Theresa says her years with the BVMs feel brief.
“It went just like that,” she says, snapping her fingers. “I loved what I was doing. I loved who I was. And I loved the BVM Community.”
Her faith remains rooted in a simple conviction:“I believe there’s a plan for each of us,” she says.
For Theresa, that plan unfolded in a life dedicated to service, language, and love.
texts.6:
## BRIGID MARY HART, BVM
Growing up in Milwaukee, Brigid Mary Hart, BVM did not see herself as particularly “Irish,” even though her family roots traced directly to Ireland. As a second-generation Irish American, she remembers the culture around her differently from friends of hers whose families had immigrated more recently.
“We were American,” Brigid Mary says. “It was no big deal about being Irish.”
**A Milwaukee Childhood**
The neighborhood where she grew up was driven more by religion and culture than by ethnicity.
“We lived in an upper-class neighborhood that was really Jewish and Catholic,” she recalls.
Yet even as a child, Brigid Mary was quietly absorbing lessons about the broader world. She later reflected on memories she did not fully understand at the time—like seeing Black domestic workers, acutely aware of unwritten “sundown” rules, hurriedly getting to the bus stop so they could get home before dark.
“You begin to think about class and about some of the hidden prejudices that were part of the culture,” she says.
Those reflections would become part of Brigid Mary’s lifelong awareness as she began her vocation.
**A Vocation That Wouldn’t Go Away**
Brigid Mary attended Holy Angels Academy, where the joyful presence of the sisters left a deep impression.
The example of the sisters she encountered as a student struck a chord. She noticed not only their commitment to their work, but the balance they seemed to live.
“They enjoyed being with the students,” Brigid Mary recalls. “But they also liked going home for prayer and being with their community.”
Still, religious life was not part of her carefully planned future. In fact, Brigid Mary had already enrolled at Clarke University in Dubuque, Iowa, and was looking forward to campus life.
Then, rather unexpectedly, she thought that perhaps somebody was trying to tell her something.
“I needed to get God off my back,” she says with a laugh. “So I came to Mount Carmel for a few weeks. And I never left.”
**Expanding Horizons**
Like many BVM sisters, Brigid Mary began her ministry in education, but traditional classroom teaching was not where her greatest passion lay.She began exploring other possibilities within education. That search eventually led her to Montessori training—a discovery that changed the course of her ministry.
texts.7:
## BRIGID MARY HART, BVM
“Montessori was my favorite ministry,” she says. “Creating the environment for learning, that was something I really loved.”
She found joy in designing classrooms that encouraged curiosity and independence. Watching children become absorbed in their work was one of the most rewarding parts of the ministry.
“They were delightful,” she says of her students. “Especially when they would get involved and get lost in their world. Concentration took over.”
Brigid Mary taught in Iowa and New York before going to Colorado, where she spent nearly 30 years. She served in parish schools, parish ministry, and in Montessori classrooms.
Those years also broadened her experience in ways she never expected. Opportunities for travel and study enriched both her faith and her understanding of the wider world.
“There were chances to do things I might never have done otherwise,” she says.
She participated in a study trip that included time in Rome and two weeks in Israel, and she has also spent time in the Philippines and the West Indies.
“You meet different people and experience different cultures,” she says. “Those experiences give you perspective and add a lot of richness to your life.”
**A Life of Faith and Openness**
Brigid Mary eventually returned to the Midwest, spending 15 years in Chicago working in a variety of ministries. At Wright Hall, a senior residence for the BVM Community, she served as activities director. She also worked in ESL programs, parish ministry, and assisting the Cenacle Community of women religious.
Throughout her years of ministry, Brigid Mary often followed her curious nature. Her willingness to sometimes step into the unknown allowed her to grow, learn, and remain energized in her work. She embraced each new chapter with openness, thankful for the opportunities to explore her interests and find her passions.
Today in retirement, she continues to explore—especially reading and art. She has taken icon writing workshops and enjoys creative expression, even if she modestly says her work is “dabbling.”
Looking back, Brigid Mary doesn’t describe her vocation as a dramatic calling. Instead, guided by faith and curiosity, it unfolded step by step with that decision to, as she jokingly says, “get God off my back.”
texts.8:
## KATHERINE “KATE” (ST. WILMA) KEATING, BVM
Katherine “Kate” Keating, BVM is very straightforward about her life and her vocation: “I’ve not disliked it ever. And I had a good time—most of the time.”
**Windy Cindy Roots**
Chicago born and bred, Kate grew up in Humboldt Park on the city’s west side—a neighborhood of immigrant faith and fierce parish loyalty. Our Lady of the Angels was her family’s parish and school. It was close enough to Kate’s house that she walked home for lunch every day.
Her father William, who died when Kate was in high school, had grown up in the same church, making her and her older brother second-generation parishioners. For Kate, faith was woven into daily life with devotion and humor.
“There were three churches in the neighborhood,” Kate remembers. “The Polish church, the Slovak church, and Our Lady of the Angels.”
Kate’s mother, Sarah, who played the organ and sang in the choir, often went to the Polish church for confession.
“The priest didn’t speak English,” Kate explains. “She would say, ‘I can go to confession, and he won’t understand anything.’”
The story still makes her laugh.
When the devastating Our Lady of the Angels fire occurred in 1958, Kate was two years into her novitiate in Dubuque, Iowa.
“My mother still lived in the parish,” she recalls. “We knew families. We knew kids.”
**From the Diamond to the Motherhouse**
Kate began her BVM journey in 1956 at age 18. But it was not necessarily her first choice at the time. A gifted baseball player, she announced to her mother that she was going to join the Bloomer Girls, a professional women’s team.
“My mother said, ‘Over my dead body,’” Kate laughs. “So I said, ‘Then maybe I’ll join the BVMs.’ That made her happy.”
Behind Kate’s humor was a call nurtured by 12 years of BVM education, and especially by one teacher.
“There was always a favorite nun,” Kate says. “Mine was Sister Paula Kelly. She taught biology. I hated biology, but I loved her.”
**Good Trouble**
BVM life wasn’t always a perfect fit for a young woman who loved baseball, noise, and jokes.
texts.9:
## KATHERINE “KATE” (ST. WILMA) KEATING, BVM
“I broke all the rules,” she admits.
Silent Sundays were difficult for Kate. Playing baseball on the lawn in front of the Mother General’s office in full habit earned a reprimand.
Still, Kate says, “They kept me.”
**Jokes and Tough Streets**
Kate earned a degree in mathematics and spent many years teaching. She particularly enjoyed junior high students.
“They say junior high kids are tough,” she recalls. “But I really liked them. They were good. I’d give them two extra points on tests if they told me a joke. That helped some kids pass.”
Her ministries carried her across Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, and Montana. In Lincoln, Neb., she started a girls’ softball team using Chicago’s unique 16-inch ball.
“I carried that ball in the trunk of my car all the time,” she says. “People had never seen anything like it.”
After earning a master’s degree in education administration, Kate spent five demanding years as the principal of St. Joseph School in Chicago’s Cabrini-Green neighborhood.
“It was rough,” she says. “But you went to those buildings. You walked up the stairs. You showed up. You talked to the parents.”
Kate knew that immersion in community life was important for the success of her students.
**A Life Lived Fully**
In retirement, Kate’s spirituality deepened through hospice ministry. For 10 years, she sat with the dying so others could rest.
“That was a very moving experience,” she says. “It was a marvelous experience.”
One night, she and other hospice workers sang to a dying woman from Ireland who requested songs from her childhood.
“She was so grateful,” Kate recalls. “It was like prayer.”
Her love for Chicago remains as strong as ever. A lifelong sports fan, she and her good friend, Dorothy Gaffney, BVM drove to Wrigley Field from Dubuque after the Cubs won the 2016 World Series to soak in the atmosphere of the victory parade.
Today, Kate stays active in Schola and enjoys the company of her BVM sisters. When looking back on her missions, she notes that they were “97.2% wonderful and 2.8% ugh.”
texts.10:
## KATHERINE “KATE” (ST. WILMA) KEATING, BVM
Kate intentionally chooses community life: “I like the doors open. I like hearing people.”
As for what 70 years as a BVM means, she answers simply: “I’ve had a good life. I’ve met good people. And I’ve never been sorry.”

**Composer, poet, musician, writer**
